newsitem.title: USA: Ford says negotiations "intensify" in labor talks.
newsitem.headline: Ford says negotiations "intensify" in labor talks.

text.p: Bleary-eyed negotiators for Ford Motor Co. and the United Auto Workers stepped up talks on Sunday for a new national labor contract, as anxious workers held back from striking.

"They've intensified this afternoon," Ford spokesman Jon Harmon said of the talks, which moved sluggishly toward the end of the first full day following the expiration of Ford's UAW contract at midnight EDT Saturday.

Ford and UAW sources also confirmed on Sunday that they reached a tentative agreement covering about 750 salaried workers represented by the union, including designers and product development employees. Details of that agreement were not immediately available.
"The tone remains constructive," Harmon said of the talks covering Ford's 105,000 hourly UAW workers. "I'm optimistic for a settlement without a work stoppage."
He declined to discuss issues still unresolved, but union officials said they believed that major economic, job and subcontracting issues were still on the table.

The union has sought to guarantee minimum employment levels and provisions that restrict the company's ability to shift work to outside suppliers, including establishing the right to strike over such decisions.
Although the union did not formally extend the Ford contract, it urged workers to report to work as normal.
A number of Ford parts plants were operating normally on Sunday, but production of cars at Ford's 15 U.S. assembly plants were not scheduled to resume until Monday morning.
At UAW local halls around the country, union officials awaited word of a settlement but remained prepared to strike.

"Hopefully they'll put something together today. People are getting pretty anxious," said John Kimbro, president of UAW Local 737 at Ford's glass plant in Nashville, Tenn. "Nobody really wants to go out on strike."

After a nearly 24-hour negotiating session starting on Saturday, a number of the approximately 400 people negotiating the pact left Ford World Headquarters early on Sunday to get a few hours' sleep, and returned later in the morning.

Early optimism that a Ford pact would be sewn up well before the deadline gave way to the realities of complex bargaining. Harmon said the 1,200-page contract document was subject to hundreds of changes that could be prompted by an agreement on a major provision.

Dale Brickner, associate director of Michigan State University's labor relations department, said Sunday that more negotiating time may have been needed to make sure that the UAW can also sell the pattern contract to General Motors Corp. and Chrysler Corp..
"They may be going slower to make sure that everybody's on board when they reach an agreement," Brickner said.
The UAW, with nearly 400,000 workers at all three companies, extended contracts at GM and Chrysler while it concentrated on Ford.

Jerry Klein, president of UAW Local 248 in Kansas City, Mo., said on Saturday night that negotiators were having difficulty reaching agreement on issues related to outsourcing -- or transferring work to outside suppliers.
The UAW wanted the right to strike when it disagreed with the company's decisions to transfer such work, which would give it greater leverage to preserve jobs.
In the last UAW contract negotiations in 1993, also led by Ford, it took a 40-hour bargaining session lasting nearly 24 hours past the deadline to produce a settlement.
Negotiations between the UAW and the "Big Three" ran past contract expiration deadlines in each of the past three pacts -- 1987, 1990 and 1993.
